chapters.title: Counting steps (Big-O and reading the limits)
chapters.tagline: Before you write a line, the input size tells you which algorithm is allowed
goals: Count how many steps a loop takes, as a function of n
Name the common growth rates: 1, log n, n, n log n, n², 2ⁿ
Read a problem's limits and know the slowest solution that still passes
Replace a double loop with one pass, using a little maths
chapters.prelude:
import time

def timed(fn, *args):
    """Run fn(*args) and return (result, seconds)."""
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
Two correct programs can differ by a factor of a million in speed. Timing them on your laptop with 10 items tells you nothing: both finish instantly. What matters is how the work grows when the input gets bigger. That's what Big-O describes: drop the constants, keep the shape.

A computer does roughly 10⁸ simple steps a second (pure Python is slower, nearer 10⁷). Every problem on LeetCode or Codeforces states its limits, like 1 ≤ n ≤ 200 000, and a time limit of 1 or 2 seconds. Put those together and you know what kind of solution the setter expects before you've read the rest.

blocks.name: ds-bigo
blocks.title: How fast each kind of algorithm grows
blocks.goal: Solve all three puzzles: for each limit on n, pick the most work you can afford in about a second.
blocks.intro: Click any bar to see an example of that kind of algorithm and how long it would take.

blocks.html: Count how many times the innermost line runs. A loop over range(n) runs n times; a loop inside a loop multiplies.
Every pair (i, j) with i < j is counted once: n(n−1)/2 pairs. That's about n²/2, and Big-O drops the ½: it's O(n²).

blocks.q: How many times does the loop body run, as a function of n? while n > 1: n = n // 2
blocks.why: Each step halves n. Starting from a million, you reach 1 after about 20 halvings, because 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶. Halving is the signature of O(log n).

blocks.q: for i in range(n): for j in range(0, n, 2): ... What's the Big-O?

opts.t: O(n² / 2), which is different from O(n²)

blocks.why: The inner loop runs n/2 times for each of n values of i: n²/2 steps. Constant factors like ½ are dropped, so it's O(n²). (They still matter in practice, but they never change which bar you're on.)

blocks.q: for i in range(n): j = 1; while j < n: j *= 2. What's the Big-O?
blocks.why: The outer loop runs n times; the inner one doubles j, so it runs about log₂ n times. n × log n.

sections.title: One pass instead of two loops

blocks.html: The most common speed-up in all of DSA: instead of looking back at every earlier item, remember a summary of what you've seen so far (the smallest, the sum, the count). Then each new item costs O(1).

blocks.title: best_profit
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. prices[i] is a share's price on day i. You may buy on one day and sell on a later day, once. Write best_profit(prices) returning the most money you can make (0 if every choice loses money). n can be 200 000, so trying every pair (buy day, sell day) is too slow.
blocks.tests:
assert best_profit([7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]) == 5, "buy at 1, sell at 6"
assert best_profit([7, 6, 4, 3, 1]) == 0, "prices only fall: don't trade"
assert best_profit([2]) == 0
assert best_profit([3, 3, 3]) == 0
assert best_profit([1, 9, 0, 5]) == 8, "the later low (0) doesn't beat 9 - 1"
big = list(range(5000, 0, -1))
r, secs = timed(best_profit, big)
assert r == 0
assert secs < 0.25, f"took {secs:.2f}s on 5 000 days: that's the O(n²) double loop. Keep the lowest price so far instead."
hints: On each day, the best sale is today's price minus the lowest price before today. Keep that lowest price in a variable as you walk.
Two variables, one loop: lowest = min(lowest, p) and best = max(best, p - lowest).
blocks.solution:
def best_profit(prices):
    lowest = float("inf")
    best = 0
    for p in prices:
        lowest = min(lowest, p)
        best = max(best, p - lowest)
    return best

blocks.title: The largest and second-largest in one pass

blocks.html: The decoys show the trap: when a new maximum arrives, the old maximum becomes second. Overwrite first before saving it and it's gone.

blocks.title: missing_number
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. nums holds n different numbers from 0..n, so exactly one number in that range is missing. Return it, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space (no set, no sorting).
blocks.tests:
assert missing_number([3, 0, 1]) == 2
assert missing_number([0, 1]) == 2
assert missing_number([1]) == 0
assert missing_number([9, 6, 4, 2, 3, 5, 7, 0, 1]) == 8
big = list(range(20000)); big.remove(12345)
r, secs = timed(missing_number, big)
assert r == 12345
assert secs < 0.2, f"{secs:.2f}s: `k not in nums` scans the whole list each time, so this is O(n²)"
hints: 0 + 1 + … + n = n(n+1)/2. The total of what's there is sum(nums). The difference is the missing number.

blocks.html: k not in nums looks like one step but it's a hidden loop over the list. Spotting hidden loops (in on a list, list.index, list.remove, slicing, string += in a loop) is half of Big-O in Python.

blocks.q: Which of these is not O(1) in Python?
blocks.why: in on a list checks items one by one: O(n). On a set or dict it's O(1) on average, because they hash. That's the whole of chapter 3.

blocks.title: pair_products
blocks.prompt: Codeforces style. Given a list a of up to 2·10⁵ integers, return the sum of a[i] * a[j] over all pairs i < j. The double loop is 2·10¹⁰ steps. Find an O(n) way.
blocks.tests:
assert pair_products([1, 2, 3]) == 1*2 + 1*3 + 2*3
assert pair_products([5]) == 0
assert pair_products([]) == 0
assert pair_products([-1, 4, 2, -3]) == -4 - 2 + 3 + 8 - 12 - 6
big = list(range(1, 4001))
r, secs = timed(pair_products, big)
s = sum(big); assert r == (s * s - sum(x * x for x in big)) // 2
assert secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s: too slow, that's the O(n²) double loop"
hints: Each x gets multiplied by every number before it. That's x * (sum of the earlier numbers). Keep the running sum.
Another route: (a₁ + … + aₙ)² = Σaᵢ² + 2·Σ_{i<j} aᵢaⱼ, so the answer is (sum(a)**2 - sum of squares) // 2.
blocks.solution:
def pair_products(a):
    total = 0
    seen = 0
    for x in a:
        total += x * seen
        seen += x
    return total

blocks.code:
calls = 0
def f(n):
    global calls
    calls += 1
    if n > 1:
        f(n // 2)
        f(n // 2)
f(16)
print(calls)

blocks.html: Each call makes two calls on half the size. The levels have 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 calls: 31 in total, about 2n. Not every recursion is slow; it depends how fast the problem shrinks. (Chapter 5 builds this from scratch.)

blocks.q: A problem: "1 ≤ n ≤ 18. Choose some of the n items so their weights sum to exactly W." What does the limit tell you?

opts.t: Trying every subset is allowed: 2¹⁸ ≈ 260 000 subsets

blocks.why: n ≤ 20 is the setter saying "brute force over subsets is fine." Small limits are a hint, not an accident.

blocks.title: A "will it scale?" checker for a team's code
blocks.client: A start-up whose search page was fast in testing and timed out on launch day with 50 000 users
blocks.brief: Build scale.py that takes a function and an input generator, runs the function at sizes n = 1 000, 2 000, 4 000, 8 000, … (stopping when one run takes more than 2 seconds), and reports the growth: "looks like O(n²): at your production size of 50 000 this takes about 40 s". Fit the slope of log(time) against log(n): a slope near 1 is linear, near 2 quadratic. Add it to the test suite so a slow change fails the build.
blocks.why: Performance bugs pass every functional test and only show up at real sizes. Doubling the input and watching the time is how engineers spot O(n²) before users do; the same idea (benchmarks in CI) runs at every large tech company.

Estimate the exponent from the timings
Predict the time at a production size
Fail loudly when the exponent jumps between two versions
stretch: Repeat each timing a few times and take the minimum (noise only ever makes things slower)
Tell n log n apart from n (it needs a wider range of sizes)

blocks.title: growth_exponent
blocks.prompt: Write growth_exponent(sizes, seconds): given input sizes and how long each run took, return the slope of the best straight line through the points (log n, log t) (least squares), rounded to 1 decimal. A slope of 2.0 means time grows like n².
hints: On a log-log plot, t = c·nᵏ is a straight line with slope k. Least-squares slope: Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) / Σ(x−x̄)².
blocks.solution:
import math

def growth_exponent(sizes, seconds):
    xs = [math.log(n) for n in sizes]
    ys = [math.log(t) for t in seconds]
    mx, my = sum(xs) / len(xs), sum(ys) / len(ys)
    slope = sum((x - mx) * (y - my) for x, y in zip(xs, ys)) / sum((x - mx) ** 2 for x in xs)
    return round(slope, 1)

blocks.title: predict_time
blocks.prompt: Write predict_time(n0, t0, k, n): a run at size n0 took t0 seconds and time grows like nᵏ. Return the predicted seconds at size n, rounded to 2 decimals.
blocks.tests:
assert predict_time(8000, 0.64, 2, 50000) == 25.0
assert predict_time(1000, 0.5, 1, 4000) == 2.0
assert predict_time(100, 0.01, 3, 1000) == 10.0
hints: Ten times the input with k = 2 is a hundred times the time: t0 * (n / n0) ** k.
blocks.starter:
def predict_time(n0, t0, k, n):
    return t0
blocks.solution:
def predict_time(n0, t0, k, n):
    return round(t0 * (n / n0) ** k, 2)

blocks.q: s = "" then for w in words: s += w. In the worst case, what can this cost for n words?

opts.t: O(n²) characters copied, because strings can't be changed in place

blocks.why: Each += may build a brand-new string and copy everything so far. "".join(words) copies each character once: O(total length).

blocks.q: An O(n²) solution takes 1 second at n = 10 000. About how long at n = 100 000?
blocks.why: 10× the input, squared: 100× the time. Doubling n doubles an O(n) program and quadruples an O(n²) one.

blocks.q: Which grows fastest as n gets large?
blocks.why: Any exponential beats any polynomial in the end. 2ⁿ passes n¹⁰ at about n = 59 and never looks back.

blocks.q: a.sort() followed by one loop over a. Total?
blocks.why: Add the steps: n log n + n. Keep only the biggest term: O(n log n).

blocks.q: for i in range(n): if i in seen_set: ... where seen_set is a Python set. Total?
blocks.why: A set lookup is O(1) on average (it hashes), so n lookups cost O(n). With a list instead of a set, the same line would be O(n²).

blocks.q: A problem allows n ≤ 10¹⁸. What kind of solution is it asking for?

opts.t: A formula, or something that halves (O(log n)) like binary search or fast power

blocks.why: You can't even loop to 10¹⁸. The answer must come from maths or from cutting the problem in half each step.

blocks.title: allowed_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: allowed(n) returns the most work you can afford for that n: "n!" up to 10, "2^n" up to 20, "n^3" up to 500, "n^2" up to 5 000, "n log n" up to 10⁶, "n" up to 10⁸, else "log n".
hints: Seven if lines, smallest limit first.
blocks.starter:
def allowed(n):
    pass
blocks.solution:
def allowed(n):
    if n <= 10: return "n!"
    if n <= 20: return "2^n"
    if n <= 500: return "n^3"
    if n <= 5000: return "n^2"
    if n <= 10**6: return "n log n"
    if n <= 10**8: return "n"
    return "log n"

blocks.q: What does Big-O measure, and how do you use a problem's limits to choose an algorithm?
blocks.a: Big-O describes how the number of steps grows as the input size n grows, ignoring constant factors: a loop over n items is O(n), two nested loops over all pairs O(n²), halving each step O(log n), trying every subset O(2ⁿ). A computer does roughly 10⁸ simple steps a second (pure Python closer to 10⁷), so the limit on n tells you the most work you can afford: n ≤ 20 allows 2ⁿ, n ≤ 5 000 allows n², n up to about 10⁶ needs n log n or better, and huge n needs O(log n) maths. To speed something up, keep a running summary (lowest so far, running sum) instead of looking back at every earlier item, and watch for hidden loops like x in list.

chapters.title: Arrays in one pass
chapters.tagline: Keep a small summary as you walk, and swap in place instead of building new lists
goals: Find the maximum-sum stretch of an array in one pass (Kadane)
Use a write pointer to filter an array in place
Rotate and reverse in place with O(1) extra memory
Sort three kinds of value in one pass (the Dutch flag)
chapters.prelude:
import time, random

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
An array is a row of boxes in memory, side by side. Reading a[i] is instant because the computer jumps straight to box i. Most array problems are about walking that row once while carrying a few numbers in your head.

The classic: which stretch of neighbouring numbers (a subarray) has the largest total? Think of a shop's profit and loss per day, and the best run of days to show investors.

blocks.name: ds-kadane
blocks.title: Every stretch, or one walk
blocks.goal: Run try every stretch to the end, then run Kadane to the end and compare how many stretches each looked at.
blocks.intro: Click any number to see why it helps or hurts a stretch.

blocks.html: The idea in one sentence: if the run you're carrying has a negative total, drop it, because adding a negative start to anything only makes it smaller.

blocks.code:
a = [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]
run = 0
for x in a:
    run = max(x, run + x)
    print(run, end=" ")

blocks.html: run = max(x, run + x) is the same rule written another way: either extend the run with x, or start fresh at x, whichever is bigger. The answer is the largest run ever seen (6, for 4 -1 2 1).

blocks.title: Kadane's algorithm
blocks.tests:
assert max_subarray([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]) == 6
assert max_subarray([-3, -1, -2]) == -1
assert max_subarray([5]) == 5

blocks.html: The first decoy is the classic bug: starting best at 0 gives the wrong answer when every number is negative (the best stretch is then the single largest number, not an empty one).

blocks.q: a = [-3, -1, -2]. What should max_subarray(a) return if a stretch must contain at least one number?
blocks.why: The best you can do is the single number -1. A version that starts best = 0 returns 0, which is only right if empty stretches are allowed. Always check the all-negative case.

blocks.title: max_subarray_where
blocks.prompt: An interview classic, one step harder. Write best_stretch(a) returning (total, start, end) for the maximum-sum subarray (inclusive indices). If several stretches tie, return the one that starts earliest, and among those the shortest. a has at least one number and can have 10⁵ of them.
blocks.tests:
assert best_stretch([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]) == (6, 3, 6)
assert best_stretch([-3, -1, -2]) == (-1, 1, 1)
assert best_stretch([2, -2, 2]) == (2, 0, 0), "ties: earliest start, then shortest"
assert best_stretch([1, 2, 3]) == (6, 0, 2)
big = [random.randint(-50, 50) for _ in range(5000)]
r, secs = timed(best_stretch, big)
assert r[0] == sum(big[r[1]:r[2] + 1])
assert secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s: too slow, use one walk"
hints: Carry run and the index start where the current run began. When run is negative, reset run = 0 and start = j before adding a[j].
Only replace best when the new total is strictly bigger: that keeps the earliest, shortest one on ties.
blocks.starter:
def best_stretch(a):
    return (0, 0, 0)

sections.title: Filtering in place: the write pointer

blocks.html: Building a new list costs memory. Many interview questions say "do it in place". The pattern: one index reads every item, another (w, the write pointer) marks where the next kept item goes.

blocks.title: move_zeroes
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. Move every 0 in the list a to the end, in place, keeping the other numbers in their original order. Return nothing; change a itself.
blocks.tests:
a = [0, 1, 0, 3, 12]; move_zeroes(a); assert a == [1, 3, 12, 0, 0]
a = [0]; move_zeroes(a); assert a == [0]
a = [4, 2]; move_zeroes(a); assert a == [4, 2]
a = [0, 5, 0]; b = a; r = move_zeroes(a); assert b == [5, 0, 0] and r is None, "change the list itself, don't return a new one"
hints: Walk with x. Every non-zero goes to a[w], then w += 1. Afterwards, fill from w to the end with zeros.
blocks.starter:
def move_zeroes(a):
    return [x for x in a if x != 0] + [0] * a.count(0)

blocks.title: dedupe_sorted
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. a is sorted. Remove duplicates in place so the first k slots hold each distinct value once, in order, and return k. (What's after slot k doesn't matter.)
blocks.tests:
a = [1, 1, 2]; k = dedupe_sorted(a); assert k == 2 and a[:k] == [1, 2]
a = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4]; k = dedupe_sorted(a); assert k == 5 and a[:k] == [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
a = []; assert dedupe_sorted(a) == 0
a = [7]; assert dedupe_sorted(a) == 1 and a == [7]
hints: Because it's sorted, a duplicate always sits right after its twin. Compare a[i] with the last value you kept, a[w - 1].
blocks.starter:
def dedupe_sorted(a):
    return len(set(a))

blocks.code:
def reverse(a, lo, hi):
    while lo < hi:
        a[lo], a[hi] = a[hi], a[lo]
        lo += 1
        hi -= 1

a = list("ABCDEFG")
reverse(a, 0, len(a) - 1)
print("".join(a))
blocks.title: Reverse with two pointers

blocks.html: Rotating right by k (the last k items move to the front) looks like it needs a second list. It doesn't: reverse the whole thing, then reverse the first k, then reverse the rest.

blocks.code:
a = list("ABCDEFG")
k = 3
def rev(lo, hi):
    while lo < hi:
        a[lo], a[hi] = a[hi], a[lo]
        lo, hi = lo + 1, hi - 1
rev(0, 6); print("".join(a))
rev(0, k - 1); print("".join(a))
rev(k, 6); print("".join(a))

blocks.title: rotate_bug
blocks.prompt: This rotation works for small k but crashes or gives the wrong answer when k is bigger than the list (rotating 7 items by 10 is the same as rotating by 3), and when the list is empty. Fix it.
blocks.tests:
a = list("ABCDEFG"); rotate(a, 3); assert "".join(a) == "EFGABCD"
a = list("ABCDEFG"); rotate(a, 10); assert "".join(a) == "EFGABCD", "10 steps on 7 items = 3 steps"
a = list("ABC"); rotate(a, 3); assert "".join(a) == "ABC"
a = []; rotate(a, 5); assert a == []
hints: Rotating by n changes nothing, so only k % n matters. Guard the empty list first (% 0 would crash).

sections.title: Three kinds in one pass: the Dutch flag

blocks.html: Sort a list holding only 0s, 1s and 2s, in one pass, in place. Keep three regions: everything before lo is 0, everything after hi is 2, and mid walks the unknown part in between.

blocks.title: Dutch national flag
blocks.tests:
a = [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0]; sort_colors(a); assert a == [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]
a = [2, 2, 0]; sort_colors(a); assert a == [0, 2, 2]
a = []; sort_colors(a); assert a == []
a = [1]; sort_colors(a); assert a == [1]

blocks.q: In the Dutch flag, after swapping a[mid] with a[hi], why don't we move mid forward?

opts.t: The number that came from hi hasn't been looked at yet, so mid must check it
To keep the loop running longer

blocks.why: Everything after hi was unknown. The swap brings one of those unknowns to mid, and it could be a 0, 1 or 2. (After a swap with lo it's safe to move on: that slot was already checked.)

blocks.title: make_non_decreasing
blocks.prompt: Codeforces style. In one operation you may add 1 to any element. Return the minimum number of operations to make a non-decreasing (each element ≥ the one before it). n up to 2·10⁵, values up to 10⁹.
blocks.tests:

assert make_non_decreasing([1, 2, 3]) == 0
assert make_non_decreasing([5, 4, 3, 2, 1]) == 1 + 2 + 3 + 4
assert make_non_decreasing([10**9, 1]) == 10**9 - 1
assert make_non_decreasing([]) == 0
hints: Raising an element to exactly the largest value so far is always enough and never wasteful. Carry that running maximum.

blocks.title: max_product
blocks.prompt: An interview favourite that breaks Kadane. Return the largest product of a non-empty stretch of a (integers, may be negative or zero). A negative times a negative is positive, so the smallest product so far matters too.
blocks.tests:
assert max_product([2, 3, -2, 4]) == 6
assert max_product([-2, 0, -1]) == 0
assert max_product([-2, 3, -4]) == 24, "two negatives make a positive"
assert max_product([-2]) == -2
assert max_product([0, 2]) == 2
hints: Carry two runs: the biggest and the smallest product ending here. A negative x turns the smallest into the biggest.
blocks.solution:
def max_product(a):
    best = hi = lo = a[0]
    for x in a[1:]:
        cands = (x, hi * x, lo * x)
        hi, lo = max(cands), min(cands)
        best = max(best, hi)
    return best

blocks.title: leaders
blocks.prompt: A warm-up that teaches walking backwards. An element is a leader if it's strictly greater than everything to its right (the last element always is). Return the leaders in their original left-to-right order, in O(n).
blocks.tests:
assert leaders([16, 17, 4, 3, 5, 2]) == [17, 5, 2]
assert leaders([1, 2, 3]) == [3]
assert leaders([]) == []
big = list(range(6000, 0, -1))
r, secs = timed(leaders, big)
assert r == big and secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s: walk from the right, keeping the maximum seen"
hints: From the right, "greater than everything to my right" means "greater than the maximum so far".
blocks.starter:
def leaders(a):
    return [x for i, x in enumerate(a) if all(x > y for y in a[i + 1:])]

blocks.q: What does Kadane's algorithm throw away, and when?

opts.t: The smallest number, at the end
The current run, as soon as its total is negative
The best answer, when a bigger one appears

blocks.why: A run with a negative total can only lower whatever follows, so starting fresh is never worse.

blocks.q: What's the extra memory used by the write-pointer filter?

opts.t: O(k), for the k items kept

blocks.why: It overwrites the same list. That's what "in place" means.

blocks.q: Rotating 1 000 items right by 1 000 003 steps. How many steps actually matter?
blocks.why: Every 1 000 steps brings the list back to where it started: 1 000 003 % 1 000 = 3.

blocks.q: Which problem is not a "carry one summary while walking" problem?

opts.t: Best day to buy and sell a share
Counting how many pairs of equal numbers there are, without extra memory and in O(n), when the numbers are unsorted

blocks.why: The first three each need just one or two running numbers. Counting equal pairs in unsorted data needs to remember which values you've seen: that's a hash map (chapter 3), or sorting first.

sections.title: Real-world project: the best run of days

blocks.title: A "best run" report for a small business
blocks.client: A café owner with three years of daily profit and loss in a spreadsheet, preparing to talk to the bank
blocks.brief: Build bestrun.py daily.csv that prints the best stretch of consecutive days (total, start date, end date), the worst stretch (the deepest loss), and the longest streak of profitable days. Then handle the café's question about the yearly cycle: treat the year as a circle (December wraps into January) and find the best stretch on that circle.
blocks.why: "Best and worst consecutive periods" appear in finance (maximum drawdown), monitoring (longest outage), genomics (high-scoring DNA segments) and sport (best scoring run). Kadane is the engine behind all of them.

Worst stretch (the same algorithm, flipped)
Longest run of profitable days
Best stretch when the year wraps around
stretch: Report the best stretch of at least 7 days

blocks.q: Explain Kadane's algorithm and the write-pointer pattern, and why each is O(n).
blocks.a: Kadane walks the array once, carrying run = the best total of a stretch ending at the current element. For each x, run = max(x, run + x): extend the stretch, or start fresh if the old run was negative and could only drag things down. The answer is the largest run seen. Starting best at a[0], not 0, handles all-negative arrays. The write pointer filters in place: one index reads every element, w marks where the next kept element goes, so nothing is copied to a new list and extra memory is O(1). Both touch every element a constant number of times, so they're O(n), versus O(n²) for trying every start and end. Related in-place tricks: reverse with two pointers, rotate by k with three reversals (k % n), and the Dutch flag with three regions lo/mid/hi.

blocks.q: A hash table's lookup is O(1) on average. When can it be O(n)?

blocks.q: You need "pairs with a[i] + i == a[j] - j". What's the key trick?

blocks.q: How does a hash table give O(1) lookups, and what's the two-sum pattern?
blocks.a: A hash table computes a hash number from the key and uses it to choose a bucket, then only compares against the few keys in that bucket. With a good hash function and a table that grows as it fills, buckets stay tiny, so lookups, inserts and deletes are O(1) on average (O(n) in the worst case, if everything collides). Keys must be immutable, because the bucket is chosen from the hash when the key is stored. The two-sum pattern: walk the array once; for each x, ask whether its partner (target − x) has been seen, then store x. Storing counts instead of indices counts pairs. More generally, rewrite a pair condition so one side depends only on i and the other only on j (for example a[i] − i == a[j] − j), then count with a dict as you walk: O(n) instead of O(n²).

blocks.html:
A shop has ten years of daily sales, and the manager keeps asking: "what did we sell between day 1 200 and day 1 450?" Adding up the range each time is slow when there are many questions. Instead, build the running total once: P[k] = the sum of the first k days. Then

sum of days l..r = P[r+1] − P[l]

because everything up to day r, minus everything before day l, leaves exactly the days in between.

def subarray_sum_k(a, k):
    seen = Counter({0: 1})
    run = count = 0
    for x in a:
        run += x
        count += seen[run - k]
        seen[run] += 1
    return count

blocks.solution:
def divisible_subarrays(a, k):
    seen = Counter({0: 1})
    run = count = 0
    for x in a:
        run = (run + x) % k
        count += seen[run]
        seen[run] += 1
    return count

blocks.solution:
def product_except_self(a):
    n = len(a)
    out = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = left
        left *= a[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= right
        right *= a[i]
    return out

blocks.q: Why does the prefix array start with P[0] = 0?

opts.t: To make it the same length as the input
So a range starting at index 0 is P[r+1] − P[0] with no special case

blocks.q: "Count subarrays with sum exactly k" when numbers can be negative. Which tool?

blocks.q: A difference array update "add 5 to positions 3..8" changes how many entries of D?

blocks.q: Explain prefix sums, the prefix-sum + hash-map trick, and difference arrays.
blocks.a: A prefix array P has P[0] = 0 and P[k] = a[0] + … + a[k-1]. Building it is O(n); then any range sum a[l..r] = P[r+1] − P[l] in O(1), because the total up to r minus the total before l leaves just the range. The leading zero removes edge cases. To count subarrays summing to k, note that l..r works exactly when P[l] = P[r+1] − k, so walk once keeping a dict of how many times each prefix sum has appeared (starting {0: 1}) and add the count of run − k at each step: two-sum on prefix sums, which works with negative numbers. Equal remainders mod k give subarrays divisible by k. A difference array does the opposite: to add v to a[l..r], do D[l] += v and D[r+1] −= v; one prefix sum at the end applies every update, so u updates cost O(u + n). In 2D, S[i+1][j+1] = grid[i][j] + above + left − above-left, and a rectangle is four lookups by inclusion-exclusion.

chapters.title: Recursion and the call stack
chapters.tagline: Solve a problem by trusting a smaller copy of it, and remember answers you've already found
goals: Write a recursive function with a base case and a smaller step
Trace the call stack and predict the order things happen
Spot repeated work and remove it with a memo
Turn deep recursion into a loop when the stack would overflow
chapters.prelude:
import sys, time
from functools import lru_cache

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version, and has a base case small enough to answer directly. The leap of faith: while writing fact(n) = n * fact(n - 1), assume fact(n - 1) already works.

Underneath, each call gets a frame on the call stack (its own n, its own local variables, and where to return to). A call can't finish until the calls it made have finished, so frames pile up and then unwind.

blocks.name: ds-recur
blocks.title: The call tree and the call stack of fib(6)
blocks.goal: Run plain recursion to the end, then run with a memo and compare how many calls did real work.
blocks.intro: Step slowly at first: watch the stack on the right grow as calls start, and shrink as they return.

blocks.code:
def fact(n, depth=0):
    print("  " * depth + f"fact({n}) starts")
    result = 1 if n <= 1 else n * fact(n - 1, depth + 1)
    print("  " * depth + f"fact({n}) returns {result}")
    return result

fact(4)
blocks.title: Watching frames open and close

blocks.code:
def show(n):
    if n == 0:
        return
    print("before", n)
    show(n - 1)
    print("after", n)

show(3)

blocks.html: Everything before the recursive call happens on the way down (3, 2, 1); everything after it happens on the way back up, in reverse (1, 2, 3). That's how the stack lets recursion "remember" where it was.

blocks.q: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?

opts.t: It loops forever, using no extra memory
Each call opens a new frame until Python's limit (about 1 000) and raises RecursionError
Python detects it and stops at the first call

blocks.why: Frames take memory, so infinite recursion runs out of stack. Python sets a limit (sys.getrecursionlimit()) to fail cleanly instead of crashing.

sections.title: When the stack is too deep

blocks.html: Python's stack holds about 1 000 frames. A recursion that goes n levels deep fails at n = 10⁵, even with a memo. Contest solutions in Python usually turn such recursions into loops: compute small answers first and build up. That's a bottom-up table, the other face of dynamic programming.

blocks.title: ways_134
blocks.prompt: Codeforces style. Count the ways to write n as an ordered sum of 1s, 3s and 4s (so 1+3 and 3+1 are different), modulo 1 000 000 007. n up to 10⁵, so recursion would overflow the stack: build the answers from 0 upwards in a list.
blocks.tests:
assert ways(1) == 1
assert ways(3) == 2, "1+1+1, 3"
assert ways(4) == 4, "1+1+1+1, 1+3, 3+1, 4"
assert ways(5) == 6
r, secs = timed(ways, 100000)
assert secs < 0.5 and 0 <= r < 1_000_000_007
hints: w[i] = w[i-1] + w[i-3] + w[i-4] (skipping negative indices), starting from w[0] = 1 (one way to make 0: take nothing).
blocks.solution:
def ways(n):
    MOD = 1_000_000_007
    w = [0] * (n + 1)
    w[0] = 1
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        w[i] = (w[i - 1] + (w[i - 3] if i >= 3 else 0) + (w[i - 4] if i >= 4 else 0)) % MOD
    return w[n]

blocks.q: How many frames are on the stack at the deepest point of fact(5)?
blocks.why: fact(5) waits for fact(4), which waits for fact(3)… down to fact(1): five frames at once. Stack depth = depth of the recursion, not the number of calls.

blocks.q: Plain recursive fib(n) makes about how many calls?
blocks.why: Each call makes two more, and the tree only gets one level shorter on one side. With a memo it's n + 1 calls doing real work.

blocks.q: power(x, n // 2) * power(x, n // 2) instead of computing half once. What's the cost?

opts.t: O(n): the two calls double at every level, undoing the halving

blocks.why: log n levels, doubling each time: 2^(log n) = n calls. Store the result once.

blocks.q: Which is a good sign that memoization will help?

opts.t: The same arguments are passed to the function many times
The function has two base cases

blocks.why: Memoization only helps when calls repeat. Hanoi has no repeats (every call has different pegs or sizes that matter), so a memo wouldn't help it.

blocks.q: A recursion needs depth 10⁵ in Python. Best fix?

opts.t: Rewrite it as a loop that builds answers bottom-up (or keep your own explicit stack)

blocks.why: Raising the limit can crash the interpreter (the real C stack runs out). Bottom-up loops have no depth at all.

blocks.title: A `du`-style folder size report
blocks.client: A video editor whose 2 TB drive is full and who can't tell which project folders are the culprits
blocks.brief: Build du.py FOLDER that walks the folder tree and reports each folder's total size (its files plus all its subfolders), the 10 biggest folders, and the deepest path. A folder's size is only known after all its children are measured, which is exactly the "after the recursive call" part of recursion. Then rewrite the walk with an explicit stack so a ridiculously deep folder tree can't overflow Python's stack.

blocks.q: Explain how recursion uses the call stack, and when and how to use memoization.
blocks.a: A recursive function answers a small base case directly and otherwise calls itself on a smaller input, trusting that call to be right. Each call gets a frame on the call stack holding its arguments, locals and return point; a frame can only finish after the calls it made finish, so code before the recursive call runs on the way down and code after it runs on the way back up in reverse. Stack depth equals recursion depth, and Python allows about 1 000 frames, so very deep recursion raises RecursionError; then rewrite it bottom-up as a loop or use an explicit stack. When the same arguments recur (like fib, where the call tree has about 1.6ⁿ calls), store each answer the first time in a dict (or lru_cache) and return it on repeats: only one call per distinct argument does work, so fib becomes O(n). Halving the input (fast power) gives O(log n) calls, but only if the half result is computed once.
